Stated Claim / Post Context:
The Ceaseless Ceasefire

For the Palestinians, the ceasefire in Israel’s war on Gaza might not be all-out war — but it’s certainly not peace, and no end is in sight.

Actual Article Body:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Gaza, “peace,” and surviving a zombie conflict.

All across the world, people are trapped by forces far beyond their control. Handcuffed by situations which they are powerless to change.

I spent countless hours talking to people like this from Southeast Asia to North Africa. Their immediate circumstances couldn’t have been more different. They hailed from radically dissimilar backgrounds; they were of different races, ethnicities, and religions. But they were bound together by one unifying force: organized, armed violence. Or, rather, the imposition of it upon them. These people were just living their lives when war arrived on their doorsteps.

When most people think of war, they think of armed soldiers. But I think of grandmothers and toddlers. Modern war zones are much more the province of civilians than combatants, even if the traditional “battlefield” has made a significant reappearance this century. Soldiers die. Civilians die in droves. Soldiers deploy here and there. Civilians are put to flight, en masse, often again and again. When memories of war invade my thoughts, I remember the tween whose hand was cut off, the farmer who dug his own grave and survived his execution, the paralyzed man who had to be left behind as troops attacked the village, the 2-year-old who survived a machete attack. Since World War II, such innocents have overwhelmingly been the main victims of armed conflict.

Being a war reporter taught me that ordinary people have extraordinary capabilities. I found that people the world over had the capacity to endure the unbearable and the survive the unthinkable. What they often cannot do, however, is push back on the source of their oppression and suffering. People can run from soldiers, but they cannot outrun war. The “safety” of a refugee camp is still an extension of the war zone. You can flee violence but still remain trapped by conflict.

Today, in her inaugural article for TomDispatch, Safia Southey — an international lawyer and expert on how societies reckon with wartime abuses — examines the plight of Palestinians in Gaza imprisoned by a conflict that refuses to die, the truce ostensively meant to save them, and the outside authorities that have trapped them in this “zombie conflict.” In this singular piece, Southey offers a window into the perverse mechanics of this ceaseless ceasefire cycle and what it would take to break it.

—Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch
